analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fee on phone bills that pays for internet discounts for schools, libraries, and clinics.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 7 Republican cosponsors to kill the "e-rate" phone fee that funds internet discounts for schools and libraries, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the part of the Communications Act of 1934 that requires telephone companies to provide discounted internet and phone connections to schools, libraries, and health care providers — the program known as the "e-rate," funded through contributions from carriers that show up as a fee on customers' phone bills. Eliminating it would spare phone companies those contributions and modestly lower phone bills, but it would end the federal subsidy that connected schools and libraries to the internet in the 1990s.
analysis.who_benefits: Telephone carriers would be relieved of a mandatory contribution to the universal service fund, and their customers would pay less on their phone bills, since carriers pass these contributions through to ratepayers. But the savings per household are small, while the program being eliminated is the one that paid to wire schools, libraries, and rural health clinics for internet service — a benefit that falls hardest on low-income and rural communities.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement that telecommunications carriers contribute to the fund that provides discounted internet and telecom connections to schools, health care providers, and libraries, freeing the companies from that obligation.
Because carriers pass universal service contributions through to customers as a fee on phone bills, repeal would slightly lower what ordinary households pay each month.

analysis.who_pays: Schools, libraries, and health care providers would lose the discounted connections the fund provides, and the students, library users, and rural patients who depend on them would lose the internet access those discounts made possible. The losses are concentrated in low-income and rural communities, where the subsidy was often the difference between being connected and not.
analysis.who_pays_short: Schools, libraries, and rural health clinics

drawbacks.text: Repeal would end the e-rate program, which provided discounted internet connections to schools, libraries, and health care providers — cutting off subsidized access in exactly the places least able to pay full price.

The savings to individual phone customers would be modest, while the program's loss would be concentrated on students, library users, and rural patients — so repeal trades a small, broad consumer benefit for a large, targeted loss to public institutions and the communities they serve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side clearly outweighs the benefit. Lowering a few dollars of monthly fees is real but small, while eliminating the e-rate would have dismantled the main federal effort to connect schools and libraries to the internet at the moment that connection was becoming essential — with the harm falling on low-income and rural communities first. An honest supporter would have to concede that calling this a consumer tax cut understates what consumers would be giving up.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to a House subcommittee and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1999, never getting a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner introduced the bill on June 10, 1998, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce.
Seven Republican colleagues signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats did.
On June 29, 1998, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, where the action history ends — no markup, no floor vote.
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired without further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Schools, libraries, and health care providers came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, the e-rate discounts that paid for their internet connections survived. Telephone carriers also came out ahead in the sense that the funding requirement they opposed stayed in place — but it was the program's beneficiaries, not the bill's target, who were protected by its death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Schools and libraries that kept e-rate funding

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the FCC's authority to require carrier contributions for school, library, and health care internet connections.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Publicly championed the schools-and-libraries internet program funded by the fee this bill would repeal, making repeal politically difficult.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter on record — the sponsor and all 7 cosponsors — was a Republican, and no Democrat signed on; the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would show a fuller split.

industries.note: If passed, the bill would have freed carriers from mandatory contributions to the universal service fund, which they pass through to customers as a phone-bill fee — a direct gain to the industry and a small saving to households. The bill failed, so carriers' obligation remains. Their interest runs partly with consumers on price but against the public program the fee finances.

industries.industry: Internet and telecom providers serving schools, libraries, and rural clinics
industries.note: These companies sell the discounted connections funded under section 254 of the Communications Act; repeal would have stripped away a subsidized customer base of schools, libraries, and health care providers. The program's survival keeps that public demand intact.
